title: Rof Gremolata
author: Pierre Thiam with Jennifer Sit (Lake Isle Press, ‘Senegal’)
desc: Finely chopped parsley, scallions, garlic, a seeded half Scotch bonnet and lemon zest — a raw finishing condiment made in a bowl, kept a week in the fridge.
longDesc: Thiam’s rof gremolata is the finishing condiment for his lamb shank mafé, distinct from rof (SEN011), the herb-and-chile stuffing used inside the fish for ceebu jën. A bunch of parsley, three scallions, two garlic cloves and half a seeded Scotch bonnet are finely chopped and combined in a bowl with the grated zest of one lemon, seasoned with salt and pepper. It makes 1 cup and keeps up to a week, airtight in the fridge. No cooking, no time or heat.
ingredients: 1 bunch parsley, leaves finely chopped — the bunch is not weighed or measured in the source
1/2 Scotch bonnet pepper, seeded and finely chopped
Fine sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Gently combine the parsley, scallions, garlic, Scotch bonnet and lemon zest in a small bowl.
Season to taste with salt and pepper. Store airtight in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.
chefTips: Wear gloves for the Scotch bonnet.
‘1 bunch parsley’ is the source’s own measure; use a bunch of normal supermarket size.
commonMistakes: Blending to a paste: gremolata is chopped.
Zesting the pith of the lemon.
Making it long ahead — the herbs lose colour.
healthBenefits: Parsley and lemon zest are rich in vitamin C and K.
culturalNote: Not the same preparation as rof (SEN011), the Wolof herb stuffing; this one is a finishing condiment from Thiam’s later work. The Yolélé ‘Senegalese Rof Dip’ page (not published here) cools Thiam’s ‘fiery, herbaceous sauce’ with Greek yoghurt and has a list/method mismatch (habanero in the method only).
sources: Source: Pierre Thiam with Jennifer Sit, ‘Senegal: Modern Senegalese Recipes from the Source to the Bowl’ (Lake Isle Press, 2015), as printed on the Lake Isle Press page and on WBUR Here & Now. Yield ‘Makes 1 cup’. TWO-PASS, agreement.
Flagged: ‘1 bunch parsley’ is unmeasured by weight or volume; salt and pepper ‘to taste’.
